title: Debt
hookLine: split it into easy payments? a householder's four happinesses, and two readings of the loan
tomorrow: how would you know you have enough?

cards: Checkout pages offer it on almost anything now: split it into easy payments, nothing due today. Sneakers, a phone, a concert ticket, a couch.
Then the little reminders start arriving, one every two weeks, long after the excitement has worn off. A trap, or a tool?
Inside the Buddhist tradition, the same question gets two honest answers, and both start from one short sutta about what makes a householder happy.

teach.b: In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha tells the merchant Anathapindika there are four kinds of happiness for someone living in the world. The happiness of having: wealth earned by effort, rightly.
The happiness of using it, on yourself, on others, on good deeds.
The happiness of owing nothing: I have no debt to anyone, small or large. And the happiness of blamelessness, a life in body, speech and mind that no one can fairly fault.
The sutta says the first three aren't worth a sixteenth part of that last one. So debt isn't the deepest worry. But freedom from it is a real joy, named on its own.

Now, two readings. The first voice points to another sutta, where the Buddha traces a chain: being poor, a person borrows; borrowing brings interest; then being pressed to pay, then being chased, then being bound.

teach.h: ONE VOICE: A LOAN IS THE FIRST LINK.
teach.b: Here a loan is the first link, and the wise move is to stay out of the chain. The second voice points to a simile the Buddha himself uses.

teach.h: ANOTHER: A LOAN REPAID, AND GLADNESS.
teach.b: A man takes a loan and puts it into his work. The work goes well.
He pays off every old debt and has something left over. And he's glad. Here, borrowing for honest work, and repaying it, can be the road to the very freedom the first sutta praises.
Both voices land in the same place: the happiness is owing no one. They differ on the road there.

how: Buddhist teachers who speak to householders often draw on AN 4.62's four happinesses when they talk about money; how to handle borrowing is left to each household's judgment, weighed against the happiness of owing no one.

o: a promise to a monk that must be kept for life
a karmic stain carried from a past life into this one
what you owe, whose absence is a happiness of its own

games.q: four happinesses, two readings — tap the pairs.
p: no debt to anyone, small or large
a loan is the first link in a chain
a loan repaid, with something left, and glad

s: in AN 4.62, freedom from debt is the happiness above all the others
blamelessness is: the sutta says the first three aren't worth a sixteenth part of it.
the Buddha uses a repaid loan, with something left over, as a picture of gladness
a man borrows for his work, it goes well, he pays every old debt, and he's glad.
the suttas see debt as nothing a householder needs to think about
owing nothing is named as one of a householder's four happinesses.

games.q: your uncle says every loan is a trap, full stop. you lean his way, but a fair debate states the other side at its best. what's the strongest case from the suttas?
o: the suttas say debt doesn't matter much, since blamelessness counts far more.
debt is fine as long as the lender is a friend or family member.
the Buddha's own simile: a loan put into work and repaid ends in gladness.
games.why: the second voice leans on the Buddha's own image of a repaid loan. both voices agree the happiness is owing no one; they differ on the road.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one small thing you owe: money to a friend, a borrowed book, a call you said you'd return. Notice where it sits in the body.
Then let it be settled in your mind, and feel, for a few breaths, what owing nothing is like.

wordCard.voice: Debt: what you owe someone else. Its opposite gets its own happiness in the suttas, and two readings of how to reach it.

carryVoice: Something to keep: free of debt, small or large, is its own quiet happiness. Four of five, on money.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62 (Anana Sutta, to Anathapindika: the happiness of possession, of enjoyment, of debtlessness and of blamelessness; the first three not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness)
Anguttara Nikaya 6.45 (Ina Sutta: poverty, borrowing, interest, being reproved, pursued and imprisoned, as a chain of suffering)
Majjhima Nikaya 39 (Maha-Assapura Sutta: the simile of a man who takes a loan, succeeds in his work, repays his old debts with something left over, and is glad)
